caption: "gaslighting" — 50,000+ searches this week. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the word Diana's brother used on a king.

Why: Charles Spencer's book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is out Tuesday and says Charles sounded "giddily elated" after Diana's death. Buckingham Palace answered that grief "can cloud reason… and color memory". Spencer: "It's not every day you're gaslit by a king."

What most people don't know: the word comes from Gas Light, a 1938 stage thriller where a husband dims the gas lamps and says his wife imagines it. The verb dates from 1961. Lookups rose 1,740% in 2022, Merriam-Webster's word of the year.
Very simply put: 1938 stage trick, 2022 word of the year.

slides.sub: To The Mail on Sunday, and again on ABC's Good Morning America. He called the Palace statement 'below the belt'.

slides.headline: The word comes from a *1938 play*.
slides.sub: Gas Light by Patrick Hamilton, first staged December 5, 1938, at the Richmond Theatre in London. Set in fog-bound 1880.
slides.image: A Victorian street lamp glowing in thick London fog at night, lamp in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wet pavement, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: The husband dims the *gas lamps* and says she imagines it.
slides.sub: He is searching the flat upstairs for jewels; lighting its lamps dims the rest of the house.

slides.headline: On Broadway it ran *1,295 performances* as Angel Street.
slides.sub: From December 5, 1941, still one of the longest-running plays in Broadway history.

slides.headline: The verb was first recorded in *1961*.
slides.sub: It stayed obscure for decades: The New York Times used it nine times in the 20 years after 1995.
